blocks.body:
The scribes of ancient Egypt wrote $\tfrac{2}{5}$ as $\tfrac13 + \tfrac1{15}$: apart from a few special symbols, they expressed fractions as sums of distinct unit fractions $1/n$. Such a sum is now called an Egyptian fraction. Existence is easy; the interesting questions are about economy and structure. How few terms are needed? How small can the largest denominator be? If the integers are split into finitely many classes, must one class contain denominators whose reciprocals add up to exactly $1$?

Some of these questions are elementary; the deepest results use Fourier analysis and smooth-number estimates. This lesson proves the existence theorem, works through the classical elementary arguments, and states the theorems of Croot and Bloom precisely.

blocks.title: Egyptian fraction
blocks.body:
An Egyptian fraction representation of a positive rational $q$ is an identity
$$q = \frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n_k},\qquad n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_k \text{ positive integers}.$$
The number $k$ is its length and $n_k$ its largest denominator.

Distinctness is what makes the problem nontrivial; without it, $a/b$ is just $a$ copies of $1/b$.

blocks.title: The greedy algorithm
blocks.body:
Given $q = a/b$ with $0 < q < 1$, the most natural move is to subtract the largest unit fraction that fits: the $1/n$ with $n$ as small as possible, namely $n = \lceil b/a \rceil$. Then repeat on what remains. For $4/13$: $\lceil 13/4\rceil = 4$, and $\tfrac{4}{13} - \tfrac14 = \tfrac{3}{52}$; then $\lceil 52/3 \rceil = 18$ and $\tfrac{3}{52} - \tfrac{1}{18} = \tfrac{2}{936} = \tfrac{1}{468}$. So
$$\frac{4}{13} = \frac14 + \frac1{18} + \frac1{468}.$$
Notice the numerators of the remainders: $4, 3, 2$ (before reducing). They went down by one each time. That is the whole proof that the method stops.

blocks.title: Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy theorem
blocks.body: For every rational $a/b$ with $0 < a/b < 1$, the greedy algorithm terminates after at most $a$ steps and produces an Egyptian fraction representation of $a/b$ with strictly increasing denominators. Consequently every positive rational has an Egyptian fraction representation.

blocks.title: Proof of the greedy theorem
blocks.body:
Let $n = \lceil b/a \rceil$, the least integer with $1/n \le a/b$. Since $a < b$, $n \ge 2$, and minimality gives $\frac{1}{n-1} > \frac{a}{b}$, i.e. $a(n-1) < b$. The remainder is
$$\frac{a}{b} - \frac1n = \frac{an - b}{bn},\qquad 0 \le an - b < a.$$
So the new numerator (before any cancellation, which only lowers it) is a nonnegative integer smaller than $a$. After at most $a$ steps the remainder is $0$.

The denominators strictly increase: the remainder is less than $\frac{1}{n-1} - \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}$, so the next denominator $n'$ satisfies $1/n' < 1/(n(n-1))$, giving $n' > n(n-1) \ge n$.

For an arbitrary positive rational $q$, use the divergence of the harmonic series: let $m \ge 0$ be the largest integer with $H_m = 1 + \frac12 + \cdots + \frac1m \le q$. If $H_m = q$ we are done. Otherwise $s = q - H_m$ satisfies $0 < s < \frac{1}{m+1}$, so the greedy expansion of $s$ starts with a denominator at least $m+2$, and all its denominators are larger than $m$. Appending it to $1 + \frac12 + \cdots + \frac1m$ gives a representation with distinct denominators.

blocks.title: Non-uniqueness and the cost of greed
blocks.body:
Representations are never unique. The identity
$$\frac1n = \frac1{n+1} + \frac{1}{n(n+1)}$$
splits any term with $n \ge 2$ into two larger-denominator terms, and applying it to the largest denominator keeps all denominators distinct. (The one representation it cannot split, $1 = \frac11$, can first be replaced by $\frac12+\frac13+\frac16$.) So every positive rational has infinitely many representations.

The greedy algorithm is short in steps but can be wildly wasteful in size. It writes
$$\frac{5}{121} = \frac1{25} + \frac1{757} + \frac1{763309} + \frac1{873960180913} + \frac1{1527612795642093418846225},$$
whereas $\frac{5}{121} = \frac1{33} + \frac1{121} + \frac1{363}$. Denominators roughly square at each greedy step, because the remainder after subtracting $1/n$ can be as large as about $1/n^2$. Finding the shortest representation, or the one with smallest largest denominator, is in general a hard search problem, and most of the classical questions in [[combinatorial-nt]] about Egyptian fractions are about these extremal versions.

blocks.title: The harmonic numbers are not integers
blocks.body: Show that $H_n = 1 + \frac12 + \cdots + \frac1n$ is not an integer for any $n \ge 2$. In particular $1$ is the only integer that is a sum $\frac{1}{1}+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n$ of an initial run of unit fractions.
blocks.solution:
Let $2^k$ be the largest power of $2$ with $2^k \le n$; since $n \ge 2$, $k \ge 1$. Among $1, \dots, n$, only $2^k$ is divisible by $2^k$: the next multiple of $2^k$ is $2^{k+1} > n$, and multiples $3\cdot 2^k, 5 \cdot 2^k,\dots$ are larger still.

Let $L = \operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$; then $2^k \,\|\, L$. Multiply $H_n$ by $L$:
$$L H_n = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{L}{j}.$$
For $j = 2^k$, $L/j$ is odd. For every other $j$, the power of $2$ in $j$ is less than $k$, so $L/j$ is even. Hence $L H_n$ is odd. If $H_n$ were an integer, $L H_n$ would be a multiple of $L$, which is even. Contradiction.

The same idea, choosing a prime that divides exactly one denominator to the highest power, is the standard tool for showing that sums of unit fractions avoid integers.

blocks.title: Odd denominators
blocks.body:
(a) Show that if $1 = \sum_{i=1}^{k} 1/n_i$ with all $n_i$ odd (distinct or not), then $k$ is odd.

(b) Show that with distinct odd denominators at least $7$ terms are needed, and verify the representation
$$1 = \frac13 + \frac15 + \frac17 + \frac19 + \frac1{11} + \frac1{15} + \frac1{35} + \frac1{45} + \frac1{231}.$$
blocks.solution:
(a) Let $L = \operatorname{lcm}(n_1, \dots, n_k)$, which is odd. Multiplying by $L$ gives $L = \sum_i L/n_i$. Each $L/n_i$ is a divisor of an odd number, hence odd, so the right side is a sum of $k$ odd numbers and has the parity of $k$. The left side is odd. So $k$ is odd.

(b) The denominators are distinct odd integers at least $3$, so the sum of $k$ of them is at most the sum of the $k$ largest available unit fractions, $\frac13 + \frac15 + \cdots + \frac{1}{2k+1}$. For $k = 6$ this is $\frac13 + \frac15 + \frac17 + \frac19 + \frac1{11} + \frac1{13} = \frac{43024}{45045} < 1$. So $k \ge 7$, and by (a) $k$ is odd.

For the identity, put everything over $\operatorname{lcm}(3,5,7,9,11,15,35,45,231) = 3465$. The numerators $L/n_i$ are
$$1155,\ 693,\ 495,\ 385,\ 315,\ 231,\ 99,\ 77,\ 15,$$
which add up to $3465$. So the sum is exactly $1$, with $9$ terms (odd, as it must be).

blocks.title: The Erdős–Straus conjecture
blocks.body:
How short can a representation be? Every $2/n$ with $n$ odd has length two: $\frac{2}{n} = \frac{1}{(n+1)/2} + \frac{1}{n(n+1)/2}$. For numerator $4$, Erdős and Straus conjectured around 1948 that three terms always suffice:

For every integer $n \ge 2$ there are positive integers $x, y, z$ with $\dfrac{4}{n} = \dfrac1x + \dfrac1y + \dfrac1z$.

The conjecture is open. (Here $x, y, z$ need not be distinct; this is the traditional form of the problem.) Two simple observations shape all work on it. First, it is enough to treat primes: if $\frac4p = \frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z$ then $\frac{4}{pm} = \frac1{xm}+\frac1{ym}+\frac1{zm}$, and every $n \ge 2$ other than a power of $2$ has an odd prime factor, while $4/2 = 1/1 + 1/2 + 1/2$ and $4/2^j$ for $j \ge 2$ is $1/2^{j-2}$ split as $\frac{1}{2^{j-1}} + \frac{1}{2^j} + \frac{1}{2^j}$. Second, many residue classes are settled by polynomial identities, as in the next example.

Mordell showed that such identities settle every $n$ except possibly those with $n \equiv 1, 121, 169, 289, 361$ or $529 \pmod{840}$. These six classes are exactly the squares $1^2, 11^2, 13^2, 17^2, 19^2, 23^2$ modulo $840$, and there is a quadratic-residue reason why no identity of this polynomial type can handle a class of squares. Computer searches have confirmed the conjecture for every $n$ up to very large bounds, but a proof for all primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$ remains out of reach.

blocks.title: Easy cases of Erdős–Straus
blocks.body: Prove that $\dfrac{4}{n} = \dfrac1x + \dfrac1y + \dfrac1z$ has a solution in positive integers whenever $n \ge 2$ and $n \not\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, and also whenever $n \equiv 2 \pmod 3$. Conclude that the only primes left open by these identities are those with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.
blocks.solution:
If $n = 4k+3$: the identity $\frac{4}{n} - \frac{1}{k+1} = \frac{4(k+1) - n}{n(k+1)} = \frac{1}{n(k+1)}$ gives $\frac4n = \frac{1}{k+1} + \frac{1}{n(k+1)}$. Split the second term with $\frac1m = \frac1{m+1} + \frac1{m(m+1)}$ to get three terms.

If $n = 4k$: $\frac4n = \frac1k = \frac{1}{2k} + \frac{1}{4k} + \frac{1}{4k}$.

If $n = 4k+2 = 2m$ with $m = 2k+1$ odd: $\frac4n = \frac2m = \frac{1}{k+1} + \frac{1}{m(k+1)}$ (the length-two formula above, since $(m+1)/2 = k+1$), and split one term as before.

If $n = 3k + 2$: $\frac{3}{n} - \frac{1}{k+1} = \frac{3k+3-n}{n(k+1)} = \frac{1}{n(k+1)}$, so
$$\frac4n = \frac1n + \frac{1}{k+1} + \frac{1}{n(k+1)}.$$

A prime $p$ not covered has $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ (so $p \ne 3$) and $p \not\equiv 2 \pmod 3$, hence $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. Together, $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$.

One more identity goes further. If $n = 8k+5$, then $\frac4n - \frac{1}{2(k+1)} = \frac{8(k+1)-n}{2n(k+1)} = \frac{3}{2n(k+1)}$, so
$$\frac4n = \frac{1}{2(k+1)} + \frac{1}{n(k+1)} + \frac{1}{2n(k+1)}.$$
A prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ is $1$ or $13 \pmod{24}$, and $13 \bmod 24$ means $p \equiv 5 \pmod 8$; so only $p \equiv 1 \pmod{24}$ survives. Continuing with identities modulo $5$ and $7$ leads to Mordell's six classes modulo $840$.

blocks.title: Colourings and density: Croot and Bloom
blocks.body:
A different family of questions asks not for short representations of a given number but for representations of $1$ inside a prescribed set of denominators. The number $1$ itself must be excluded from the allowed denominators, since $\frac11 = 1$ trivially.

Erdős and Graham asked whether, whenever the integers $2, 3, 4, \dots$ are coloured with finitely many colours, there is a finite set $S$ of one colour with $\sum_{n\in S} 1/n = 1$. This is a Ramsey-type statement in the spirit of [[ramsey-arithmetic]]. Croot proved it in 2003.

blocks.title: Croot's colouring theorem (2003)
blocks.body:
For every $r \ge 1$ there is $N(r)$ such that for every colouring of $\{2, 3, \dots, N(r)\}$ with $r$ colours there is a monochromatic set $S$ with
$$\sum_{n \in S} \frac1n = 1.$$

blocks.title: Bloom's density theorem
blocks.body:
A colouring statement usually has a density strengthening: one colour class in a finite colouring has positive upper density, so it is natural to ask whether every set of positive upper density already contains such an $S$. Erdős and Graham conjectured this, and Bloom proved it in 2021.

Bloom's theorem. If $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has positive upper density, that is $\limsup_{N\to\infty} \frac{|A \cap [1,N]|}{N} > 0$, then there is a finite $S \subseteq A$ with $\sum_{n\in S} 1/n = 1$.

He in fact proved a quantitative version in which the hypothesis is that $\sum_{n \in A,\, n \le N} 1/n$ is large compared with $\log N$ times a slowly decaying factor. A density result implies the colouring result (some colour class has positive upper density), so Bloom's theorem contains Croot's qualitatively (a compactness argument passes from colourings of all of $\{2,3,\dots\}$ to the finite form).

Why analysis enters. To find $S \subseteq A$ with $\sum_{n\in S} 1/n = 1$, one fixes a common multiple $Q$ of the candidate denominators and asks for $\sum_{n\in S} Q/n = Q$, an equation among integers. The number of subsets $S$ satisfying it can be written as an integral over $\theta \in [0,1]$ of a product $\prod_n (1 + e(\theta Q/n))$ times $e(-\theta Q)$, where $e(t) = e^{2\pi i t}$. Showing that this count is positive means showing that the main contribution (from $\theta$ near rationals with small denominator) beats everything else, in the style of the [[circle-method]] and of the Fourier proofs in [[arithmetic-progressions]]. For this to work the denominators must be chosen with many small prime factors, so that $Q$ stays manageable; this is where estimates for smooth numbers ([[smooth-powerful]]) come in. Croot developed this approach and Bloom refined it to handle density. We do not give the proofs.

- Forgetting distinctness: $\frac23 = \frac13 + \frac13$ is not an Egyptian fraction; $\frac23 = \frac12 + \frac16$ is.
- Allowing the denominator $1$ in colouring problems makes them trivial; Croot's theorem colours $\{2,3,\dots\}$.
- The greedy algorithm gives a representation of length at most the numerator, but not the shortest one, and its denominators can be enormous (see $5/121$).
- In Erdős–Straus it suffices to handle primes, but Mordell-type polynomial identities cannot finish the job, because no such identity covers a class of squares.
- A parity or valuation argument shows that a given sum is not $1$ or not an integer; it never produces representations. Constructions need separate ideas.

Egyptian fractions draw on [[divisibility]] (common denominators, valuations as in [[p-adic-valuation]]) and on the extremal style of [[combinatorial-nt]]. Croot's theorem is an instance of [[ramsey-arithmetic]], and Bloom's density version follows the pattern of Szemerédi-type theorems in [[arithmetic-progressions]], with Fourier analysis and [[smooth-powerful|smooth-number estimates]] doing the work. The related question of which integers are sums of distinct reciprocals of a given set connects to [[additive-bases|complete sequences]].

1. Find the greedy expansion of $\frac{7}{15}$ and a shorter or smaller-denominator alternative, if one exists.
2. Prove that $\frac12 + \frac13 + \cdots + \frac1n$ is never an integer for $n \ge 2$, and more generally that $\frac1m + \frac1{m+1} + \cdots + \frac1n$ is never an integer for $1 \le m < n$. (Hint: use a power of $2$, or Bertrand's postulate.)
3. Show that for $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ the fraction $\frac4n$ is a sum of three unit fractions with distinct denominators.
4. Show that $1$ is not a sum of reciprocals of distinct primes.
